video_title: AI Makes Hacking Easy. But Private Hackers Can Now Strike Back at Cybercriminals
gist: Former CFTC chair Chris Giancarlo and TRM Labs' Ari Redbord explain how their crypto privateering (letters of marque) proposal led to an August White House national security memo authorizing DOJ- and Treasury-vetted private contractors to hack back transnational criminal groups like cartels and pig-butchering networks, but not state actors like North Korea. They pair this with warnings that AI has made ransomware and scams scale at machine speed, and argue for AI-driven defense, pressure on China over DPRK laundering, and keeping escalation decisions with government.

insights.claim: TRM Labs counted about 7,500 ransomware attacks in 2025 when attacks were human-in-the-loop; in 2026 fully end-to-end, human-out-of-the-loop AI ransomware attacks have appeared, meaning attack counts could scale to 75,000 or millions.
insights.speaker: Ari Redbord (TRM Labs)
insights.so_what: Attack volume is no longer bounded by human labor; defensive and insurance cost models must assume orders-of-magnitude more attempts.
insights.quote: in 2026, we've seen endtoend human out of the loop ransomware attacks.

insights.claim: TRM's August AI and crime adoption index found criminal AI adoption up about 40% year-over-year, with AI-involved scams reportedly up 13x since 2022.
insights.speaker: Laura Shin (host)
insights.so_what: AI is a measurable force multiplier for fraud, raising compliance and anti-fraud tooling demand.

insights.claim: Ari Redbord frames AI-enabled attacks on hospitals, water filtration and electric grids as a civilization-level threat rather than merely a law enforcement or national security problem, since hospitals are the largest ransomware target.
insights.speaker: Ari Redbord (TRM Labs)
insights.so_what: Critical-infrastructure cybersecurity spending is likely to become a top policy priority.
insights.quote: So this is not a a a law enforcement threat or even a national security threat. This is civilization level.

insights.claim: North Korea has stolen over a billion dollars from crypto so far this year and roughly $6-8 billion over the past six to eight years, with proceeds funding weapons proliferation.
insights.speaker: Ari Redbord (TRM Labs)
insights.so_what: DPRK remains the dominant tail risk for crypto platforms and a driver of regulatory scrutiny.

insights.claim: Ari Redbord argues North Korea, an economy of near zero, has used a cadre of cyber warriors to elevate itself to adversary status on par with Russia, China or Iran, showing the asymmetric power of cyber capabilities.
insights.speaker: Ari Redbord (TRM Labs)
insights.so_what: Cyber offense offers outsized geopolitical leverage to small states, so state-backed crypto theft will persist.

insights.claim: Laura Shin cites a week of disclosures exposing old internet infrastructure: PHP bugs (affecting WordPress backends), a Railway platform leak that let crypto be drained from stored keys, and Indian certificate authority e-Mudra using keys as weak as the number four.
insights.speaker: Laura Shin (host)
insights.so_what: Legacy infrastructure vulnerabilities are surfacing rapidly, likely AI-assisted, raising risk for any crypto stack depending on them.

insights.claim: Ari Redbord says the new wave of AI-enabled attacks is decentralized, since anyone now has access to the tools, making privateering less applicable and requiring hand-to-hand white-hat defense plus heavy cybersecurity investment.
insights.speaker: Ari Redbord (TRM Labs)
insights.so_what: Offense-defense balance shifts toward defenders who adopt AI fastest; privateering is not a fix for diffuse attackers.
insights.quote: anyone has access now to tools and it becomes much more decentralized and quite frankly much more difficult

themes.theme: Crypto privateering: from op-ed to NSPM

insights.claim: Chris Giancarlo and Chris Perkins of Franklin Templeton proposed in a Cointelegraph op-ed reviving the US Constitution's letters of marque and reprisal (Article I, Section 8 Congressional power) to let private actors hack back state-sponsored hackers like the Lazarus Group.
insights.speaker: Chris Giancarlo (former CFTC chairman)
insights.so_what: Shifts the US cyber posture debate from defense to offense with private-sector participation.
insights.quote: Why not modernize it from the 21st century and unleash the really the awesome innovation capability of our own private sector

insights.claim: Giancarlo pitched crypto privateering at the March 2025 White House crypto summit, where it drew strong interest from Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick and especially Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, followed by briefings to Treasury, law enforcement, the House Agriculture Committee and senators.
insights.speaker: Chris Giancarlo (former CFTC chairman)
insights.so_what: Shows a direct line from crypto-industry advocacy to executive cyber policy.

insights.claim: In August the White House issued an order (a National Security Presidential Memorandum) authorizing vetted private-sector government contractors to conduct offensive cyber operations, grounded in the Computer Fraud and Abuse Act rather than the Constitution's letters of marque power and without going to Congress.
insights.speaker: Chris Giancarlo (former CFTC chairman)
insights.so_what: Creates a new contracting market for offensive cyber capability among vetted firms.

insights.claim: Under the memo, each private hack-back authorization must be signed off by both the Department of Justice and the Treasury Department, and targets are limited to non-state criminal actors.
insights.speaker: Chris Giancarlo (former CFTC chairman)
insights.so_what: Tight dual sign-off means slow, selective deployment and a small set of eligible contractors.
insights.quote: each authorization needs to be signed off by the Department of Justice and the Treasury Department

insights.claim: The presidential memo set October 11 as the date for DOJ and other agencies to issue implementing rules; Giancarlo had not seen them published but believes the government is actively drafting terms and may be disseminating them quietly to contractors.
insights.speaker: Chris Giancarlo (former CFTC chairman)
insights.so_what: Offensive operations may already be underway without public disclosure; watch for contractor announcements.
insights.quote: it's very possible that they may be disseminating them in a quiet fashion

insights.claim: Giancarlo calls the White House approach directionally right but incremental, and expects further action following the recent wave of hacks, with possible expansion of scope in future orders.
insights.speaker: Chris Giancarlo (former CFTC chairman)
insights.so_what: The program's scope is likely to widen over time if early operations succeed.
insights.quote: I think it's a first step. Um I think it's a good step.

insights.claim: Giancarlo says the NSPM is more prudent and mature than his own unrestricted privateering proposal, admitting he almost felt embarrassed by proposing it without such restrictions.
insights.speaker: Chris Giancarlo (former CFTC chairman)
insights.so_what: Even the proposal's author endorses guardrails, signaling durable bipartisan-style acceptance rather than reversal.
insights.quote: what came back was actually a very mature, thoughtful document

insights.claim: The NSPM opens by asserting that the American private sector's scale, speed and capacity secure a critical offensive cyber advantage for the United States.
insights.speaker: Ari Redbord (TRM Labs)
insights.so_what: Policy explicitly treats private cyber firms as strategic assets, favoring US cyber/AI security vendors.
insights.quote: The American private sector is the most innovative and techn technologically advanced in the world and its scale, speed, and capacity secure a critical offensive cyber advantage for the United States.

insights.claim: Redbord stresses guardrails: authorized privateers are DOJ-vetted contractors, often former law enforcement, controlled by what he calls the most conservative lawyers he has dealt with in 11 years at DOJ.
insights.speaker: Ari Redbord (TRM Labs)
insights.so_what: Expect the eligible contractor pool to be small and ex-government heavy.
insights.quote: these are the most conservative lawyers you could ever possibly deal with

insights.claim: Redbord notes historical letters of marque were needed because the early US had little or no navy, whereas today the US has the largest national security apparatus, which controls the privateers it deputizes.
insights.speaker: Ari Redbord (TRM Labs)
insights.so_what: Modern privateering is state-supervised outsourcing, not freelance hacking.

insights.claim: Escalation risk is the core flaw of unrestricted privateering; both guests say decisions on escalation must stay with DOJ and elected officials, with the private sector only executing government-blessed actions.
insights.speaker: Chris Giancarlo (former CFTC chairman)
insights.so_what: Reduces probability of private hack-backs triggering state conflict.
insights.quote: I think that was always the flaw perhaps in in our approach to privateeering.

themes.theme: Targets: TCOs, cartels and pig butchering

insights.claim: The privateering authority covers transnational criminal organizations such as cartels, ransomware gangs and pig-butchering scam networks, but excludes nation states like North Korea and Iran to avoid acts of war under international law.
insights.speaker: Ari Redbord (TRM Labs)
insights.so_what: Lazarus Group crypto thefts are not addressed by private hack-back; crypto firms still depend on government action against DPRK.
insights.quote: Think cartels, think ransomware groups, think so pig butchering is a great example

insights.claim: Redbord argues pig-butchering networks and transnational criminal organizations steal hundreds of billions per year, dwarfing North Korea's multi-billion crypto thefts, making them a high-impact first target.
insights.speaker: Ari Redbord (TRM Labs)
insights.so_what: The biggest fraud losses sit with scam networks, not DPRK, so enforcement impact on fraud volumes could be large.

insights.claim: Giancarlo suggests the restriction on targeting state-linked actors may force quasi-state-backed cartels to declare their government alignment, bringing transparency to who sponsors them.
insights.speaker: Chris Giancarlo (former CFTC chairman)
insights.so_what: A second-order effect could be surfacing hidden state sponsorship of criminal groups.
insights.quote: what this may force cartels to do is actually declare, "We're aligned, so leave us alone."

insights.claim: If US private hack-back gets good at hitting criminal groups, state sponsors may be deterred.
insights.speaker: Chris Giancarlo (former CFTC chairman)
insights.so_what: Deterrence spillover could reduce state-linked attacks indirectly.
insights.quote: If we get good at it, if we get good at it, we may scare off some of the state sponsors.

insights.claim: Pig-butchering compounds in Laos, Myanmar, Thailand and Cambodia use trafficked workers scamming 24 hours a day with fully digital infrastructure including cell towers and Starlink, so offensive cyber would aim to take that infrastructure down and claw back funds.
insights.speaker: Ari Redbord (TRM Labs)
insights.so_what: Infrastructure providers like telecom and satellite internet become enforcement chokepoints.

insights.claim: The US government's action against the Prince Group, a Cambodian transnational criminal organization linked to the highest levels of the Cambodian government and Chinese intelligence, produced the largest forfeiture in history, cited as $10-15 billion.
insights.speaker: Ari Redbord (TRM Labs)
insights.so_what: Shows large-scale crypto forfeiture is feasible, a precedent for clawback-oriented operations.

insights.claim: Hackers and scammers have rarely been hacked themselves, so their defenses are likely weak and early US private-sector offensives could have outsized impact before they harden.
insights.speaker: Chris Giancarlo (former CFTC chairman)
insights.so_what: Early-mover advantage for offensive contractors; effectiveness likely decays as targets adapt.

insights.claim: The privateering idea originated with Giancarlo's former chief of staff Mike Gill as a tool against drug cartels, and Senator Lee has a cyber letters of marque bill that started in a cartel-only context, reflecting the administration's day-one designation of cartels as terrorist organizations.
insights.speaker: Ari Redbord (TRM Labs)
insights.so_what: Legislative path for broader letters of marque exists via Congress.

insights.claim: Privateering need not be only retaliatory; it can be used preemptively against identified actors engaged in cyber-enabled crime such as scam compounds, even absent a direct cyber attack on the US.
insights.speaker: Ari Redbord (TRM Labs)
insights.so_what: Broadens the scope of potential operations beyond incident response.

insights.claim: Infrastructure takedowns like the covert operation of the Hansa darknet market show the model: because volume and speed make case-by-case enforcement impossible, authorities must map networks and seize servers.
insights.speaker: Ari Redbord (TRM Labs)
insights.so_what: Network-level disruption beats one-off arrests for scaled crime.
insights.quote: it's almost impossible based on the volume and the speed to go after individual cases

insights.claim: Redbord says Lazarus Group is not state-sponsored but is the North Korean state itself, so North Korea is off the table for private privateers today.
insights.speaker: Ari Redbord (TRM Labs)
insights.so_what: Crypto firms should not expect private hack-back recovery of DPRK thefts like Bybit.
insights.quote: It it's not state sponsored. It is the state

insights.claim: Giancarlo argues the state-actor restriction is not disarmament: private firms can hand capabilities to the Department of Defense or other agencies, which pull the trigger.
insights.speaker: Chris Giancarlo (former CFTC chairman)
insights.so_what: Private cyber capability still flows into state operations against DPRK via contracting.
insights.quote: The question is just who pulls the trigger.

insights.claim: Redbord argues China is the key lever against North Korea: pressure China to crack down on Chinese banks and money laundering organizations that launder DPRK funds, sanction Chinese banks that facilitate it, and cut off Chinese purchases of North Korean coal.
insights.speaker: Ari Redbord (TRM Labs)
insights.so_what: Secondary sanctions on Chinese banks are a plausible escalation path with market implications.

insights.claim: As a prosecutor, Redbord served a Patriot Act subpoena on a Chinese bank involved in North Korean money laundering; because non-compliance means losing US correspondent banking, a death penalty for a global bank, it ultimately produced records.
insights.speaker: Ari Redbord (TRM Labs)
insights.so_what: Correspondent banking access is a powerful extraterritorial lever beyond cyber.
insights.quote: the penalty for non-compliance is that we can cut off their correspondent banking, which is essentially a death penalty for a a global bank

insights.claim: Redbord first noticed Bitcoin around 2015-2016 when North Korea laundered it in cases also involving counterfeit $100 bills and cigarettes, framing crypto as just the latest target of a criminal regime.
insights.speaker: Ari Redbord (TRM Labs)
insights.so_what: DPRK crypto theft is a structural feature of the regime, not a crypto-specific anomaly.

insights.claim: North Korea's IT worker scheme now uses real-time deepfake videos in live hiring interviews, as warned by 11 agencies across countries in July; employers increasingly require new hires to come to headquarters in person for about a week.
insights.speaker: Chris Giancarlo (former CFTC chairman)
insights.so_what: Remote hiring at crypto firms is an attack surface; expect in-person onboarding and identity verification spend.

insights.claim: TRM Labs launched a tool combining its blockchain data with 50 off-chain data providers (threat intel such as Flashpoint) for holistic risk, which Redbord says can be applied to detect deepfakes; he recommends every compliance team use AI.
insights.speaker: Ari Redbord (TRM Labs)
insights.so_what: Demand for AI-driven compliance and deepfake detection vendors should grow.
insights.quote: we combined it with 50 uh off-chain data providers

insights.claim: Both guests implied the recent DoS attack that knocked out North Korea's internet was deliberate, with Giancarlo saying it was no accident.
insights.speaker: Chris Giancarlo (former CFTC chairman)
insights.so_what: Suggests covert offensive action against DPRK is already occurring.
insights.quote: That wasn't just somebody tripped over a power cable in the back room.

insights.claim: Giancarlo argues containment, as with the Soviet Union and Cuba, has generally been democracies' response to closed societies like North Korea, with no easy answers.
insights.speaker: Chris Giancarlo (former CFTC chairman)
insights.so_what: Expect long-duration pressure rather than a quick resolution of DPRK crypto threats.

insights.claim: Redbord says every smart contract, operating system, water filtration facility, electric grid and hospital system needs to be scanned by AI to find vulnerabilities early, since attackers already use AI.
insights.speaker: Ari Redbord (TRM Labs)
insights.so_what: AI-powered audit and vulnerability-scanning tools are a growing must-have, including for DeFi.

insights.claim: Giancarlo argues that the many non-networked, standalone US electric grids and old nuclear plants are a hidden strength against a single network vulnerability cascading across systems.
insights.speaker: Chris Giancarlo (former CFTC chairman)
insights.so_what: Network consolidation increases systemic risk; legacy isolation has defensive value.
insights.quote: one of the protections we have is the non-networked capability of our electric grid

insights.claim: Giancarlo's CFTC enforcement maxim: regulators will always be a step behind criminals; the goal is never to be more than one step behind rather than three or four.
insights.speaker: Chris Giancarlo (former CFTC chairman)
insights.so_what: Frames realistic expectations for enforcement against AI-enabled crime.
insights.quote: our job is to never be more than one step behind the bad guys

insights.claim: AI companies already report dangerous user queries to government, per a Wall Street Journal report about people using AI to research poisoning large populations.
insights.speaker: Chris Giancarlo (former CFTC chairman)
insights.so_what: AI labs are already integrated into government security reporting, easing their use in cyber programs.

insights.claim: Redbord notes crypto security best practices are developing among developers, citing the DeFi Education Fund's work on hardening.
insights.speaker: Ari Redbord (TRM Labs)
insights.so_what: Industry self-standardization on security may preempt harsher regulation.
